Course Title: Tools for Mathematics and the Sciences: Calculus
Description:
This course will expose students to certain basic tools and calculations in calculus. Some of the material may be familiar to those who studied mathematics in high school. Familiarity with the material discussed in this course may be assumed in subsequent courses across various disciplines including mathematics and physics. 
  In an article titled ‘The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences’, physicist Eugene Wigner wrote “… the enormous usefulness of mathematics in the natural sciences is something bordering on the mysterious and that there is no rational explanation for it”. Mathematics has emerged as the natural language using which the laws governing the working of the universe can be described; it is also a discipline with a rich internal structure explored through powerful frameworks for description and justification. Whether one is studying black holes or neural networks, molecular bonds or climate models, tiling patterns or cryptography, the use of mathematics is unavoidable. A solid foundation of mathematics is therefore an essential part of the skill set required of every student of the natural sciences; a good grasp of basic tools, examples, and calculations is also essential for those planning to study mathematics in greater depth and rigour. 
  Note: This course does not count as a required or elective course contributing to the graduation requirements in either Mathematics or Physics.

The course is designed to help students understand and interpret the rationale of strategic decisions. It provides students an insight into the practice, process, and theory of making managerial decisions. Description: The word ‘Marketing’ is embedded in conversations of everyday life, and general perception that marketing is all about selling and advertising. However, marketing is a much larger concept that drives an organization with great societal impact. 4P of product, place and distribution, promotion, and price - comprise the original "Marketing Mix." Together with rigorous and complete analysis of the environment, customers, and competitors, they are the key activities of marketing management, and the crucial ones: failure to find the right combination of the "mix" often result in irretrievable product (or service) failure and severe damage to organizational finances and credibility. This course shall follow a blended pedagogy of interactive lectures, case and caselet discussions, and class activities to introduce the fundamental concepts of marketing to the participants.

Data accumulated through the operation of information systems are also further analyzed using statistical algorithms (data analytics) to reveal novel yet reliable patterns that can be exploited to improve the efficiency and quality of work processes.

Description:
This course is the first of a two-part sequence aimed at providing a thorough understanding of the concepts and methods of microeconomics. 
  
  In this course, we will study consumer behavior in detail – looking at consumer preferences, budget constraints, and the utility maximization problem in the framework of Marshallian analysis. We will then learn how consumers allocate consumption, get an insight into income and substitution effects, and derive consumer demand functions. We will take a quick look at game theory, which investigates strategic decision-making among a small group of players. We will also briefly touch upon the theory of producer behavior, beginning with a stylized model of the firm, and understanding how economists model production, and how firms minimize their costs. 
  
  Part two of the Microeconomics sequence will cover producer behavior in greater detail, and examine how producers, consumers and the government interact in different settings.

Description:
This course introduces students to mathematical and statistical techniques for conducting empirical analysis in economics. It lays the foundations for the study of techniques to estimate and test hypotheses connected to quantifiable economic relationships. Students will learn to estimate and test basic regression models. The course will also prepare students to interpret estimated regression models and enable them to explore model biases that arise because of data limitations, misspecification, heteroscedasticity, and other factors. This course is a mix of conceptual understanding and practical application. Concepts will be explored through recourse to the textbook, and class notes and discussion. These concepts will then be applied to data sets while using R, the statistical programming language. 
  
  While a deep treatment of the issues surrounding causal analysis is beyond the scope of this course, we will take a close look at the conditions necessary for causal inference while we cover the course material. Through such scrutiny, we will gain insight into when statistical relationships may be considered ‘causal’ and when merely ‘correlational’.
  
  Topics: Data types, simple regression, multiple regression, estimation, inference, asymptotics, qualitative variables, heteroscedasticity, collinearity, diagnostics, hypothesis tests, miscellaneous specification and data issues.

Description: This is a course on the economic history of Modern India, conventionally dated as the period from 1757 to the present. A serious student of economics should not shy away from controversies and unsettled issues in macroeconomics, and should have the confidence to apply his knowledge to popular and important topics like financial markets and financial crises. The focus in this course will be on certain specific topics that any serious student of economics must have knowledge of. Six topics have been chosen for inclusion in this course at an intermediate level: different approaches to macroeconomic theory, theories of business cycles, macroeconomic policy, financial markets, macroeconomic crises and economic growth theory. Course Title: Economics and Public Policy: An Introduction
Description:
Given the increasing wealth inequalities, should governments look at Universal Basic Incomes for certain sections of the society? Should AI replace low-cost jobs? Should borders be open or secured? Given rising fuel costs, should governments invest more in alternative fuels or increase subsidies for public transportation? Should government departments and enterprises (railways, airlines, telecom, petroleum) be privatized? These are examples of public policy questions that are inextricably linked to questions in economics. The goal of this introductory course is to prepare students to look at larger public policy questions of this kind and others through the lens of economics, stakeholders, resources use and resource constraints.
  This course hopes to cultivate in students an understanding of the underlying issues that influence policy. With political economy becoming the crucial issue of this century, there is a persistent need to develop a deep and specific understanding of the behavior of the markets and the actions of government and the purposes that fashion such arrangements. As the discourse between the economy, society and government becomes clear, so does the use of public policy. It then becomes a visible hand of the government to supplant the invisible hand of the market to achieve desirable societal goals. Working through monetary directions, governmental regulations, legislations, taxation and redistributed transfers, public policy aims to create a level playing field in societies to create growth and development of priority and emerging sectors. In this class, we will develop an in-depth understanding of what public policy is and why we sometimes justify government involvement in solving economic and social problems.
  This course aims to provide students with the basic tools to develop an understanding of practical and theoretical issues of the public policy process. Students will get familiar with the nature of public policy and its process, read and discuss theoretical materials explaining the public policy process and describe and analyze practical policy issues policy making - from agenda setting, policy design, policy formulation and adoption, implementation and evaluation. They will also discuss scenarios to simulate efficient and equitable outcomes and also understand the reasons behind policies failing. It will rope in economics concepts of moral hazard, free rider problems, virtue signaling among others.

This course introduces the field of political economy to institutions and economic outcomes. It will begin by addressing the definitions of institutions and frameworks of economic outcomes. It will study the interrelations between the long-term effects of institutions on economic growth and other societal outcomes. The course will delve into the significant variations in economic and political development among nations with similar appearances.
  Drawing upon historical evidence, it will examine if institutional development, even unplanned, has delivered profound and far-reaching economic consequences.
  
  This course is designed to provide students with a deeper understanding of both the institutions and organizations of the world economies and their roles in shaping divergence in the distribution of earnings, wealth, and opportunities. The course will explore the merit behind the concept that the world can pursue economic development by establishing suitable economic institutions, emphasizing the significance of private property and competition. Additionally, it will examine whether better economic outcomes happen in open and pluralistic political systems.
  
  This course will also familiarize the students with the frontiers and tools of policy research topics and complement public policy and economic development courses. It will allow the students to understand and participate in academic discussions on emerging economic issues. It will provide insights into the political and public-policy debates that address the widening inequality and possible means of addressing it.

Course Title: The Rise of Civilizations in India
Description: This course on early India explores the political, social, economic and religious developments from 2000 BCE up to 800 CE. We will move chronologically through the trimester to understand the changes and continuities that defined ancient India. At the same time, each block will be explored thematically, ranging from differing ideas of sovereignty and governance, the emergence of heterodox sects and Puranic traditions, and their inter-linkages with modes of production and social organisation, changes in material culture, craft technologies, commerce and urbanisation. Together these themes will provide an overview not only of what happened in early India, but why do we study early India? We will use a combination of primary sources and scholarship, and survey the relevant historiographical debates.

Course Title: Moving Home: Migrations in Deep Time
Description:
For millions of years, people, plants and animals have moved across continents, adapting to
 dynamic past climatic changes and responding to evolving ecological niches in multiple
 ways. This course explores the when, where, how and why of ancient population migrations
 across South Asia. Here, pre- and protohistoric populations inhabited diverse environments,
 leaving behind a wealth of evidence from which archaeologists address questions of
 interest. Who were these populations, and where did they come from? How did their use of
 space across ancient landscapes change through time? Here, we trace the story of migrations
 and mobility of prehistoric populations in South Asia. We begin our story around 3 million
 years ago in Africa and move across the world in the footsteps of hunter-gatherers, farmers
 and urban communities, culminating in the Indus Valley Civilisation. We look at evidence
 drawn from archaeology, past environmental changes, fossils and genetics. We explore
 debates in models that reconstruct the timing and nature of past migrations, on species
 involved and complexities arising from extreme events and environments. We culminate by
 discussing how archaeologists interpret migrations and the implications this has had on the
 evolution of conceptual approaches in archaeology and other disciplines.

Course Title: Modernism: The Art and Architecture of Anxiety
Description:
Modernism: The Art and Architecture of Anxiety, begins by exploring the pivotal artistic and architectural movements of the early 20th century, as attempts to find order and control in an increasingly chaotic world. A growing feeling of alienation and uncertainty about the future owing to the social upheaval of industrialization and the trauma of World War I
 prompted a widespread rejection of traditional artistic, social, and political norms in Euro- America. Modernism, in this “western” sense, was principally an exploration of new forms
 and techniques that shattered existing aesthetic modes, and established a new kind of truth or order that was centered around fragmentation.
 In the initial leg of the course students will therefore explore how the crisis of certainty in turn of twentieth century Europe, eventually led to an artistic embrace of abstraction. A sense of an intellectual and existential vacuum prompted artists to abandon representational art, as they felt that objective reality could no longer be accurately depicted. Instead, they embraced non-figurative art to express inner, subjective “truths” and new, non-Euclidean approaches towards comprehending space and time.
 
 In the second portion of this course we will examine how the anxiety undergirding the advent of Indian modernism was distinct from its Western counterpart. While European modernists grappled with the alienation of the industrial age and the fragmentation of reality, Indian artists faced a different, more complex set of concerns: the trauma of colonialism, the struggle for national identity, and the challenge of synthesizing tradition with modernity. In her influential book, "When Was Modernism," the art critic Geeta Kapur, for instance, highlights how Indian modernists were not simply rebelling against a bourgeois establishment, but were instead engaged in a "double discourse." The anxiety in this context was not about societal fragmentation but rather the existential struggle to forge a new national identity amidst the pressures of colonial rule. Indian modernists grappled with the tension between preserving cultural heritage and embracing the future, a creative anxiety that defined their artistic and architectural expressions. Drawing from Kapur’s writing, and from the art of Nasreen Mohamedi, and the architecture of Charles Correa and BV Doshi, the final leg of the course will therefore examine the extent to which abstraction in the context of Indian Modernism may be viewed as a profound effort to impose order on a world that appeared increasingly divided up between the national and the global, between the inner and the outer, and between the mind and the body.

Course Title: Sources of the Self: India in the Second Millennium A.D.
Description:
This course explores the most significant developments of medieval and early modern India. Second Millennium is also the time period when regional cultures, linguistic and literary traditions as well as popular religions were produced. It is important to note that these constructs inform our social, cultural and religious lives today and in that sense constitute our sources of the self. In that sense, our goal is to examine the medieval in our contemporary world. 
 We will study the following six themes in this course. 
 First, the emergence of regions and regional cultures, which are often based on bhashas or regional languages. While some of these languages had already been in existence for several centuries, it is mostly towards the end of the first millennium AD that Indian bhashas emerge from the shadows of Sanskrit or Prakrit and begin to be used for political, literary, religious and discursive purposes. This moment also marks the emergence of regional political formations and regional cultures, primarily based on bhashas, across India. Our first objective is to explore the emergence of bhashas, their connection to political power and the new expressive possibilities available for their speakers. Note that such linguistic and regional cultures have been the basis for linguistic states in independent India. 
 Second, we will consider the nature of state formation and imperialism across India by considering examples such as the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and Bahamani kingdoms as well as the Mughal empire. We will also study political and administrative innovations as well as the political culture produced in this period. Note that the political elites produced in this era continue to exercise their influence over South Asia until the present. 
 Third, we will study the increasing complexity and diversity of Indian religious imaginations of this era, in which Islam and Christianity become an important part of Indian religiosity. Our specific focus will be on developments in popular Hinduism, specifically bhakti religiosity in different regional languages and cultures. Additionally, we will examine the presence and spread of Islam, particularly through Sufi traditions and the question of conversion to Islam.
 Fourth, we will examine how the Indian landscape was transformed with new forms of monumental architecture, urbanism and water reservoirs, all of which were intimately connected to medieval political projects. Medieval monuments, be they temples, palaces, mosques, forts, mausoleums or water bodies, were built using enduring material and continue to be a part of the built environment. Medieval cities such as Delhi, Surat and Bangalore, though transformed during colonial and modern era, continue to inform Indian urban culture. 
 Fifth, Our final major theme will be to look at the economic developments of the Second Millennium, specifically the expansion of agriculture, manufacturing, trade and commerce and urbanization. This is the period when Indian economy is integrated into the global economy and trading networks. 
 Finally, we conclude the course by considering India’s engagement with the early modern world. Since modernity is seen as a European achievement, we want to end this course by asking whether other cultures, specifically India in our case, contributed to the making of European modernity or fashioned their own modernity. 
 Note that in our exploration of the above mentioned six themes, we will foreground the movement of people, ideas, cultural practices within India and from places such as Central Asia, Arabia, Turkey, Persia, Africa and Afghanistan, all of which leads to the remaking of Indian landscape, demography and civilization.

Course Title: Morality and Its Rationality: Aristotle & Kant
Description: An age-old moral fable places Hercules at the challenging crossroads of choices: the easy life of pleasure and the hard life of virtue. Aristotle and Kant, two distinguished philosophers from distinct time-periods, unanimously claim that the hard life of virtue alone is a worthy life. Both justify virtuous living by tracing its necessary roots back to the central core of human nature – our rationality. Yet, as has been long supposed, the disagreements between their ethical positions are conspicuously loud: Aristotle favors happiness as the highest end of virtue, while Kant considers virtue to involve duty unadulterated by happiness; Kant favors a life of action towards a human world under moral laws, while Aristotle glorifies the life of contemplation as an ideal life of an individual. Whose position is valid and tenable? How do we account for the differences in their rationalist accounts of goodness? This course aims at a critical and comparative exploration of the moral theories proposed by Aristotle and Kant. It will begin with an introduction to the broader themes and trends in the history of moral philosophy to locate Aristotle and Kant in their respective contexts. It will discuss the metaethical underpinnings of their respective moral theories: Aristotle founds his eudaimonian virtue ethics on his commitments to a purpose-driven natural world (in Physics) and to the psychology of human soul (in De Anima). Kant on the other hand derives his deontological ethics from a critique of the faculty of reason, and by grounding our morality in the idea of freedom (in the first Critique and Groundwork III). The central focus of the course will be to address the dialectic of Aristotelian ‘happiness’ and Kantian ‘duty’ through an exploration of their respective ethical theories. Students will be introduced to the central themes of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics and Eudemian Ethics including the notions of virtue (aretē), happiness (eudaimonia) and practical wisdom (phronēsis). They will also be introduced to Kant’s formulations of the moral law and the taxonomy of moral duties through selections from his Groundwork and Metaphysics of Morals. The course will also highlight the significance of Aristotle’s and Kant’s moral theories to enable students to reflect on the relevance of their ideas in today’s world.

What does freedom mean? How does it go beyond the lay definition that it lies in the ability to act and speak without constraint? What are the implications of parsing this concept at the individual level or examining it in a relational or collective way? Philosophically, the concept of freedom plays out in the domain of metaphysics and ethics, with theories ranging from the libertarian, the compatibilist, and the deterministic. These transcendental ideas have had a subtle but definite impact on our constitutional guarantees for free speech on the one hand, and the restrictions placed on them on others. What implications does the information we have about inner processes have for the issue of agency? What are the grounds, if any, for coercing opinion and behaviour through pressure? What is the space for freedom of religion in a secular state? What is the distinction between positive and negative liberty and how are these related to notions of libertarianism, collectivism, autonomy and free will? Finally, where is freedom situated in discussions on fairness and justice and what are alternative notions of freedom, for example, as a form of self-realisation or as a model for non-domination. This inter-disciplinary course touches on philosophy, constitutional law, political theory, ethics, jurisprudence and media law.

Contemporary philosophers like Jacques Ranciere, Jean Luc Nancy, Geeta Kapur, Griselda Pollock, Boris Groys, Asta and others offer varied pushes and pulls to the landscape of aesthetic discourses in the arts be it through philosophical, feminist and socio-political perspectives as well as through the critique of the very field of aesthetics from the informed by various social categories. Course Title: Debating India: Key Deliberations in the Constituent Assembly of India
Description: The Constitution of India, consisting of 395 Articles divided into 25 Parts and 12 Schedules, was crafted by the Constituent Assembly, which included 389 members from diverse social, economic, and political backgrounds. Adopted on 26 November 1949 and coming into effect on 26 January 1950, the Constitution has been amended 106 times over more than seven decades. Despite these amendments, its fundamental structure and key features, such as Fundamental Rights, have largely remained unchanged. In a nation marked by vast diversity, caste, religious and racial divisions, and significant economic disparities, this endurance of the Constitution is a remarkable achievement—both of the framers and the Indian populace who embraced its vision. What is particularly remarkable is the process through which the Constitution was crafted, encompassing the debates, counter-arguments, and justifications for each Article. At the time of its drafting, social and cultural divisions—centered on caste, religion, region, and language—along with economic inequalities, were as prevalent as they are today. Despite these deep-rooted differences, the members of the Constituent Assembly successfully created a Constitution that not only provided security and stability to a nation emerging from two centuries of colonial rule and the lasting trauma of Partition but also continues to shape the lives of individuals and communities in post-colonial India. Three key questions emerge: What were the arguments and counter-arguments behind the creation of some of the fundamental features of the Indian Constitution? How did the members of the Constituent Assembly reach a consensus on a constitutional framework for such a diverse and divided nation? And what lessons can be drawn from the Assembly's deliberations to better understand contemporary debates surrounding the same core aspects of the Constitution? A critical exploration of these questions will not only help students understand the key debates that took place in the Constituent Assembly but also encourage critical thinking, a deeper constitutional perspective, and insights into democratic approaches for addressing the challenges that continue to shape India's public life today.

The process of establishing an identity as a modern democratic sovereign state was not easy for India. Especially because this required the diversity and plurality of identities to be anchored to a common universally accepted idea or imagination of the nation. The history of india is replete with civilisational encounters and invasions. However, India distinctively transformed invasions into accommodation, rupture into continuity and division into diversity as argued by Sunil Khilnani. Thus, the success or failure of the state is deeply contingent on understanding its constraints and compulsions. It is deeply connected to the success of democracy in accommodating and nurturing the diversity of identities. Diverse identities often come in conflict with each other unsettling the democratic fabric of the state which significantly relies on the principles of liberty and equality to defend itself. Thus, the course will engage with the idea and imagination of India though contemporary debates and challenges around the working of Indian politics. Some of the debates that the course identifies are: the paradox between democracy and development, frequently raising the question of equality; caste and the question of social justice that brings under review state performance and affirmative action; religious freedom and the communalisation of politics that demands secularism be understood through democracy, equality and liberty; regionalism and secessionism that challenges territorial state sovereignty while accommodating ethnic diversity; and the universal and uniform language of representation that addresses the women’s question, nonetheless failing to accommodate the inter-sectionalities and diverse lived experiences. The course is divided into five broad units: Imagining India: Democracy and Development; Caste, Social Justice and Reservation; Religion and Communalism; Regionalism and Secessionism; and India and the Women’s Question

This course is designed as an introduction to Comparative Politics, a sub-discipline in the study
 of politics. Comparative Politics is traditionally defined in two ways. First, in contrast to
 International Relations, it used to refer to the domestic politics of countries, usually other than
 one’s own, which Political Science students would devote an entire course to. Second, it is
 defined by the use of the Comparative method, the underlying assumption of which is that all
 knowledge is relative. We learn new things with reference to what we already know, and our
 assessments are usually implicitly or explicitly relative. Comparative Politics as a field trains
 us to do this systematically with regard to matters political.
 In this course, we will step aside from both these traditional definitions. Familiarity with
 everyday ideas, such as the ‘state’ or ‘nation,’ and with the most common arrangements of
 government, will be this course’s priority. Thus, as an introduction, this course will cover
 foundational concepts, the organization of government, political systems and central political
 questions. The idea is that students who are interested in politics and who are interested in
 informed citizenship, will leave the course with clarity about the words, ideas, arrangements
 and processes that make up everyday politics—such as different kinds of legislatures or
 different levels of government or different election procedures. This clarity is the foundation
 of advanced, complex political analysis.

Course Title: The Strongmanand the Fakir: Understanding the Populist Phenomenon
Required for: Elective course for Politics Major / Minor, Politics-History Joint Major
Description: How do we understand contemporary events such as Brexit, the surge in radical right political parties, left-wing anti-austerity movements, and the rise of ‘strongman’ leaders such as Donald Trump, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Narendra Modi? Connecting these phenomena is the concept of Populism that has emerged as a buzzword in contemporary times and holds a relevance that cuts across geographical boundaries. This course discusses the different theoretical approaches to populism such as the ideational approach, the discursive approach, and the performative approach. The course also offers an empirical and contextualised focus on the varying incarnations of populism and populist leaders in global politics. It pays particular attention to the gendered content of populism as a phenomenon and the field of populism studies. The course also explores different approaches to understanding populism’s relationship with democracy, and traces possible responses to the ‘populist challenge’.

Required for: Required for Politics majors and minors
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Yes POLT 203 Politics in Multiple Frames and POLT 205 Global Politics I (Global Politics in the 21st Century: An Introduction).
Description:
How do we make sense of global politics in an era where the state appears at once both durable and highly permeable and interconnected, when the increasing power of corporations and media transcend national borders, and when the structures that determine our collective political life appear to be both institutionally obdurate and physically unsustainable?
This course builds on POLT 205 Global Politics I (formerly titled Global Politics in the 21st Century: An Introduction), focusing on contemporary challenges and systemic perspectives that have been developed to help us grasp the structures, agents, and mechanisms of global political order. We begin with an engagement with genealogies of how “the global” emerges as a domain and frame of systemic analysis, as distinct from the idea of the “international”. We move to three major conceptual domains in which global politics is theorised: structures and institutions of global democracy, governance, representation, and participation; changes in the temporalities and frameworks of conflict and its resolution – from new modes of warfare to new regimes of global justice; and the ways in which movements and flows – of people, commodities, capital, knowledge, ideas, identities, and solidarities – shape and restructure global politics.
Throughout this course, we will grapple with the question of how to identify and theorise changes, as well as to see the durable dynamics underlying changing systems, on a global scale.

Course Title: Coping with Diversity and Conflict: A Global Survey of Strategies
Prerequisites to enrol for this course:
The course is intended primarily for 3 rd -year and 4 th -year
 students, regardless of their major discipline. Some background gained in the
 required courses of the Politics major may be useful, but is not necessary.
Description:
The human kind is not homogenous. Various forms and
 degrees of ethnic and cultural diversity permeate most societies across our
 world—and often lead to conflict. The regulation of diversity and conflict is therefore
 a foremost task and challenge of governments and governance, and have been so
 throughout the era of late modernity that we live in. It is as salient as ever as the 21 st
 century completes its first quarter and enters the second.
 Coping with Diversity and Conflict: A Global Survey of Strategies is an in-depth
 analytical scrutiny of the repertoire of strategies sovereign states—and sometimes
 other actors—have used and continue to use to eliminate or regulate diversity and
 conflict in their territories and societies. The five strategies we study are: genocide,
 mass expulsion, partition, secession, and
 devolution/autonomy/federalism/consociation. Students are introduced to the terms
 and to the concepts that underlie the terms, which are then fleshed out with
 discussion of recent and current examples (case studies) drawn from across the
 world. The course will be offered in the second trimester of AY 2025-26.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course:
The course is intended primarily for 3 rd -year and 4 th -year
 students, regardless of their major discipline. Some background gained in the
 required courses of the Politics major may be useful, but is not necessary.
Description:
This course is about the most intractable genre of political
 conflict. This type of conflict arises when two or more contending entities—which
 may be nation-states, and/or communities that self-define as ‘nations’—assert
 ownership (sovereignty) over the same territory. The competing claims to ownership
 of/sovereignty over the same land have often given rise to bitter, protracted conflicts,
 viewed through a zero-sum lens by the antagonists. What is common to the
 polarized antagonists is that all invoke the right to national self-determination (NSD)
 in support of their claim. The conflicts produced by these clashing aspirations to NSD
 are highly resistant to accommodation and compromise. The violent enmities they
 often generate further entrenches polarization and condemn entire world regions to
 prolonged instability. NSD conflicts are a global phenomenon—examples are found all over the world in
 recent and current times. Structured in a comparative case-study format, this course
 looks in depth at five such conflicts in the contemporary Middle East (the case of
 Israel and the Palestinians), South Asia or the Indian subcontinent (the cases of
 Kashmir and Sri Lanka), the Balkans region or southeastern Europe (the post-
 Yugoslav case of Bosnia-Hercegovina), and western Europe (the case of Northern
 Ireland). Students are exposed to the specific histories and contexts of these cases
 but are also encouraged to think and analyze comparatively across countries and
 world regions. The course is particularly focused on the great challenges of buildingpeace processes and crafting peace settlements in NSD conflicts. The course will be
 offered in the second trimester of the 2025-26 academic year.

 students, regardless of their major discipline. Some background gained in the
 required courses of the Politics major may be useful, but is not necessary."

Course Title: Communities, Identities and Cultures in India
Required for:
Social studies Major, Social Studies Minor.
Elective for Politics
Major and Minor
Description: What is identity? How do community identities define socio-political practices? Does identity and othering go hand in hand? How do languages shape community identifications? How does popular culture inform identity formation in India? What is majoritarianism and where do we locate the minorities in India? How are diasporic identities constructed and sustained? In the course ‘Communities, Identities and Cultures in India’ we would ask several such questions and seek answers. This course intends to explore social identities and social locations in India from the perspectives of practices, diversities, and hierarchies around those practices. Expanding on the discourse of personal is political, this course aims to analyse how our everyday practices and identifications stem from larger community affiliations, which also imply stereotypes and othering. The course is divided into four parts - in the first part we will contextualise the significance of communities and identities at large, and survey how scholars have located and critiqued community as an analytical concept to investigate what collective identity might mean in India with special reference to ethnic identities, religious identities, colonialism, nationalism, and secularism. The immersive engagement in this section will deep dive into village studies, and engage with different scholarly approaches to the study of culture through festivals, ritual and other forms of community cultural expression. In the second section we will look into social construction of identities, and how community identity becomes a category of experience through the prism of social categories, cultural expression, and language. This section will also capture the pulse of linguistic nationalism as the defining point of identity assertion in India on one hand and English language elitism as an expression of colonial lingering on the other. In the third segment we will examine the role of mediation, media, and identity and community formation in the diaspora. In this section, students will also engage with transnational frameworks and diasporic identities. Having located the politics around community affiliations and collective identities in the conceptual and theoretical contexts, in the fourth and the last segment, students will undertake a small research project.

Course Title: Caste and Indigeneity Studies: Critical Perspectives from South Asia
Required for: Sociology and Social Anthropology Major and Minor
Description: This course introduces the historical social categories, processes and institutions through which social formations in the Indian sub-continent have been described, and governed. Rulers, elites, empires, governments and other formations of power on the one hand, and the experiences and negotiations of subjection and oppression on the other are discussed. Drawing on original texts, scholarly writings, discursive cultural production and social movements, the course will examine social organization in the Indian context. The course traces the epistemic trajectory of caste and indigeneity from the colonial to the contemporary period, and interrogates the complex socio-economic, political, cultural and religious institutions and processes through which caste and tribe continue to be reinscribed as everyday social experience in South Asia.

Required for: Sociology and Social Anthropology Major and Minor
Description: This course familiarizes students with diverse classical and critical perspectives to capitalism. We will explore key thinkers and draw connections with contemporary debates around the various manifestations of capitalist relations.

Course Title: Introduction to Sociological and Anthropological Thought
Required for: Social studies Major, Social Studies Minor
Description: This required course introduces students to key moments in the development of sociological and anthropological thought. Starting with the origins of the two disciplines; the ways in which both disciplines are from inception implicated in the social, historical, political and economic context out of which they emerged; we proceed to examine how ideas have emerged over time, through relentless critical inquiry and engagement with diverse and changing contexts. Each module will introduce students to a particular moment in the discourse and involve engagement with a selection of representative texts drawn from key sociological and anthropological thinkers. This is not an exhaustive course on the history of sociological/anthropological thought, nevertheless the representative selection of texts is aimed at elucidating key theoretical insights of important thinkers. Students are expected to undertake immersive reading and critically reflect on the ideas thus introduced and their relevance (or not) in the contemporary world.
Is this course prerequisites for any fut: Yes - there will be another similar curse offered in T3 and this course will be required for it.

Required for: Social Studies Major, Social Studies Minor
Description: Why does media ownership matter? Is media freedom genuinely safeguarded in democracies, or is that merely a myth? How does social media contribute to community polarization in India? What constitutes the public sphere, and to what extent is it shaped by gender? How do diasporic communities negotiate cultural identity through food and engage in political discourse via social media? In what ways do diasporic communities engage with social media for political participation, debate and mobilization, and how does this impact political dynamics in both their host and home countries ? This course seeks to critically examine these pressing questions by engaging with key theoretical and empirical scholarship at the intersection of media, politics, society, and diaspora. It will provide participants with conceptual tools to analyze how media practices are shaped by power relations, and how they, in turn, influence public life, and shape up identity. The course concludes with a project, allowing participants to apply core concepts and analytical frameworks to contemporary empirical media related issues or case studies. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, interdisciplinary engagement, and reflexive analysis.

Required for: Social Studies Major, Social Studies Minor
Description: This course provides a critical examination of globalization and its multifaceted impacts across nation-states, analysing the expanding networks that continuously reshape the contemporary world, with particular attention to structural asymmetries between the Global North and Global South. It situates globalization within historical, economic, and cultural contexts while engaging with social movements and practices emerging from transnational flows of capital, people, and ideas. The course is structured into three units. Unit 1 introduces foundational debates and conceptual frameworks in the political economy of globalization, tracing its historical evolution through key readings including Saskia Sassen, Amartya Sen, Anthony Giddens, A.G. Frank, Scholte etc. Unit 2 focuses on Indian society, examining the intersections of culture, religion, and class, drawing on the scholarship of Surinder Jodhka, Sanjay Srivastava, and others. Unit 3 explores international migration and digital media as both outcomes and drivers of globalization, engaging with Arjun Appadurai’s concept of “scapes” alongside the work of Koen Leurs, Karim H. Karim etc  to analyse diasporic formations, cultural flows, and the mediascape in shaping transnational identities and publics. The course concludes with a fieldwork-based research project, enabling participants to apply theoretical frameworks to empirical inquiry and gain hands-on experience in analysing the dynamics of globalization in contemporary contexts.

Required for: Social studies Major, Social Studies Minor
Description: Why are the young women of some communities of Tamil Nadu, for example, expected to marry their maternal uncle i.e. mama? How and why did the Kulin Brahmins of Bengal justify having numerous wives? Traditionally, amongst the Nair, women were financially independent and inherited their mother’s house. Why did British colonialism change certain laws around marriage and inheritance and how did these transform family structures as well as ideas of gender and community in South Asia? Kinship, or how people are related to each other, has been an important way of learning about them and their culture. The categories some of us might have long considered “natural” such as gendered identities, patriarchal norms, social hierarchies, and even political systems, have revealed, especially when considered in light of other cultural systems, as constructed.

Course Title: Religion and Society in South Asia
Required for: Social studies Major, Social Studies Minor
Description: This course is about the study of Religion with a particular focus on South Asian religions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Zorastrianism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism), as they have been studied anthropologically, historically and politically – as daily beliefs and practices, and in relation to wider South Asian culture, history and politics. This course will provide both a grounded study of religious practices and religions in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sikkim, Sri Lanka as well as a postcolonial critique of the study of religions and nationalism in the South Asian realm.

Required for: Global Arts Monir, Litt- Arts Joint Major, Concentration
Description:
This course will introduce the students to the wide array of
 possibilities and opportunities offered by the arts as a discipline
 beyond practice. The field of art writing and criticism is
 undergoing interesting experimentation in recent times with
 several critics and writers taking recourse to new creative forms
 in writing on art. Similarly, the arts are sustained by an interlinked
 scaffolding of supporters and allies, as can be seen in arts
 management, grant making, conservation, curation, advocacy,
 activism, journalism and scholarship. Practitioners in each of
 these fields, often called mediators or translators of the arts, help
 in the dissemination, perception, transaction, and value-creation
 of arts. In other words, they form the ecosystem within which art
 can thrive. In this course, students will learn how such mediators
 have engaged with the arts through a series of seminars, talks,
 and discussions. Through separate writing workshop modules and
 working groups, students will acquire basic skills in some of these
 practices. The course aims to instill students with a curiosity to
 explore future pathways into the arts, encouraging the use of
 their interdisciplinary skills and knowledge and expanding the
 horizon of the arts beyond professional practice into everyday
 life. This course is best augmented with the Performance
 practicum course offered as well as electives focussed in some of
 these practices.
 Learning Outcomes
 1. Introduction to various practices of mediation and
 engagement with the arts.
 2. Acquiring some basic understanding and working
 knowledge of some of these practices,
 eg. writing, curation, activism etc.
 3. Enabling future interdisciplinary pathways into the arts.

Required for: Elective for Arts, Econ and Business
Description: Understanding the creative economy, new business models for the 21st century given the digital economy, practical business concepts applicable to a value creator, culminating in a business pitch exercise for creative economy ideas to real-time investors

A practicum designed to help budding entrepreneurs especially in the creative space, and/or mentorship from real world/industry mentors towards creating original products or ideas and bringing them to fruition

Required for: Required for Global Arts Minor, Literature-Arts Major, Elective for Sociology & Social Anthropology Major and Minor
Description: This course will help students develop conceptual frameworks for exploring the arts as cultural practice and aesthetic experience. Concepts and issues in the study of expressive cultures will be introduced by drawing on periods, movements, genres and traditions from different world art cultures. The course will interweave experiential and analytical learning with socio-historic and critical interpretations, drawing on a variety of examples. Thematic units in the course include a consideration of art as experience; sensing, perceiving and feeling as cultural praxis; meaning making; social organization of cultural practices; power, identity and the politics of representation. Examples could be drawn from ancient, medieval, pre-modern, postcolonial and contemporary periods. Throughout the course, students will be encouraged to apply conceptual learnings to a cultural practice of their choice, giving them an opportunity to deepen their learnings from the course through immersive experience.

Course Title: Theatre Of The Climate: Performing A Just Future
Required for: Global Arts Monir, Litt- Arts Joint Major, Concentration
Description:
Theatre of the Climate: Performing a Just Future is an interdisciplinary course that
 bridges environmental sciences and the arts to explore climate change as both a systemic
 crisis and a human story. As climate realities become increasingly urgent, understanding
 them requires not only scientific insight but also emotional resonance, cultural memory, and
 ethical imagination. This course invites students to examine climate change through the
 lenses of social and ecological justice, considering how inequalities of caste, gender and
 geography shape vulnerability and responsibility.
 Blending systems thinking, ecological theory, and participatory art practices in theatre,
 dance, storytelling, and visual arts, students will explore the role of traditional knowledge
 systems, in making the climate crisis personal and public. Drawing on readings from
 science, performance studies, and decolonial thought, alongside engagements with artistic
 practitioners and community archives, students will develop original art-based interventions.
 The course culminates in collaborative performance prototypes that embody just and
 sustainable futures. It is ideal for students pursuing environmental sciences, global arts, or
 any other discipline with an interest in climate action and creative expression.
 Theatre, dance, and visual arts can bring to life the narratives of those affected by
 environmental injustices, offering audiences a visceral understanding of these complex
 issues.
 This course is proposed to be capped at 15 students.
 Learning Outcomes:
 1. Students will be able to analyse climate change as a “super wicked problem”
 using systems thinking and social-ecological frameworks.
 2. Students will critically engage with the intersections of climate injustice and
 social inequality through caste, gender and class lenses.
 3. Students will develop and apply performative, visual, and narrative art
 practices to sense, express, and communicate climate experiences and
 knowledge.
 4. Students will collaboratively design and present creative interventions - such
 as performances or installations - that address climate justice and imagine
 alternative futures.

Required for: Required for Literature majors and minors
Description: This course is designed to introduce Literature majors to some of the fundamental concepts and practices of literary criticism. We shall begin with a preliminary survey of the history of literary study as a way to propose working definitions of a few key terms: What do we mean by literature? What is a text? Who is an author? And what constitutes literary criticism? This last question will bring us to questions that pertain directly to method: In what ways can a text be read? Does it make sense to speak of a literary method in the same way as we speak, say, of the scientific method? Or, to put it another way, is there anything that all works of literary criticism share in common, or is it futile to look for such a common ground?

Course Title: Out on a Quest: Writing a Research Essay
Required for: Required for Literature majors and minors
Description: Researchers are questers asking research questions to better understand the worldly wilderness we inhabit. They track and read sources, reflect on ideas, form alliances, combat misreading - wielding reading skills and writing implements. They return transformed by the quest, to tell their tale with a well written research essay that adds to how we know the world. This upper-level writing course for literature students will advance the skills learned in WOC and LAA. The drafting process will include basic archival research to find sources for a topic of one’s choice; distinguishing between different kinds of sources; asking research questions; making claims supported by evidence; sustaining an argument; getting and giving revision feedback; and, learning citation systems in addition to MLA. Motivated by the guiding principles of asking questions that perhaps stay unanswered in the process of knowledge creation, this writing intensive course aims to introduce students to the work of research as it gets bigger in scale and complexity. To meet the final goal of writing a proofed and polished 2,500 words research essay by the end of the term, students will complete shorter, targeted tasks for the new skills they are learning. For instance, if they have been introduced to an online archive, or have found one on their own, they may submit a description of it. Other exercises may include annotating a text, creating a glossary of conceptual terms, close-reading, writing summaries of sources they will work with, giving peer feedback, interspersed with revising and submitting drafts at incremental word limits.

Course Title: Android Dreams: Technological Imaginaries in Literature and Film
Required for: Elective for Literature majors, minors, and concentrations
Description: Technology is particularly central to the history of modernity. But how do we think about technology in relation to ourselves? This course will move away from instrumental approaches to technology as simply objects of “innovation” and “use” or instruments measured in terms of their “effects” and “social impacts”. Instead we will analyse how literature and film help us to think about our relationship to technology. How do we live ethically with technologies? How do they make us feel? Why do we fear them? Why is technology the central site where we debate questions pertaining to the human such as creativity, autonomy, emancipation, thought and emotion?

Course Title: Make or Break?: The Literary Canon
Required for: Required for Literature majors and minors
Description: This course explores how literary canons are formed by a multitude of different forces such as nation, culture, language, and economics. Beginning with a case study on the “western” or “English” canon in the form of one of the most canonical female writers of all time, this course teaches students how, why, and when certain “great” works gain their importance or place in the canon. In doing so, students will learn how certain forces of inclusion and exclusion create so-called literary canons. This course also asks students to consider what it would mean to imagine canons (or their absence) differently: for example, what would a “global” literary canon look like? How would you structure a canon of women’s literature? Do we need canons at all? To begin to answer these questions, our reading will explore the idea of the canon and its relationship to adaptations, translations, intertextuality, and literary prizes through key writers and texts and a trio of literary events in 2025: the global celebrations of the 250th anniversary of Jane Austen; the Nobel in Africa symposium in Stellenbosch, South Africa (November 2025), featuring literary prize-winners J.M. Coetzee and Abdulrazak Gurnah; and, closer to home in south India, the 2025 International Booker Prize for Heart Lamp to Banu Mushtaq and Deepa Bhasthi

OAA Verification: Title change, so changed the course code
Required for: Required for Literature majors and minors
Description: This course aims to introduce students to Translation Studies (TS), by engaging with specific questions central to the domain. These questions revolve around the concept of equivalence, including issues of equivalence at various levels of language and text; they relate to challenges specific to non-literary and literary translations. At the same time, this course exposes students to various theoretical perspectives on translation in its interactions with culture. Beginning with a broad outline of the scope, history and central issues of TS, this course goes on to discuss various levels of equivalence. It begins with a focus on non-literary translation, and, thereafter, opens up to challenges specific to literary translation. Beginning with a close-up view in order to engage with these ‘building blocks’ of translation, it then goes on to view the process of translation from its place within culture and addresses issues that flow from it. Finally, it brings up some philosophical perspectives on translation. Thus, the course aims to give a comprehensive view of the act of translation and of issues concerning the domain of TS.

Required for: Elective for Literature majors, minors, and concentrations
Description: This course looks at representations of history in fiction, film and auto/biography. Focussing on texts in English geographically ranging from England to South Africa, India and Australia, and temporally from the eighteenth century to the present day, we will examine the intersections of history and fiction in selected works from around the globe. What are the implications of reading a novel for its historical content or accuracy? How does the memoir or biography negotiate intergenerational histories and ideas of veracity? How do different writers reflect on questions of authorship and audience? How might archival research and films – documentaries, biopics, and adaptations – expand our readings of novels and histories? This is an interdisciplinary seminar which is designed to emphasise a high level of critical thinking and creativity. Students will be encouraged through their worksheets and their ongoing notebook assignment to be fully prepared and to contribute to each session productively, as well as to reflect on connections between each week’s topic. The final assessment is a visual archive essay which will require independent and original research, and which will be workshopped and presented to the seminar group at the end of term.

Required for: Elective for Literature majors, minors, and concentrations
Description: This is a 12-week course in which students learn the nuances of editing and develop a thorough understanding of the publishing industry. By the end of the term, you will have mastered the intricacies of wielding the red pen by picking out holes in stories, learning to make every word count, and knowing your semi-colons from your commas. You will learn to differentiate between editing a short story and a news story. As expert editors, you will realize that editing is as much a science of exactitude as it’s an art. To write, you will discover, is to edit. The class will be heavy on workshops. You will learn not just to edit but to edit under pressure. You will also learn what it means to be an editor in the age of AI. Editing is a small component of the publishing journey, which is often a long, drawn-out affair. We will become familiar with this somewhat opaque process and understand the complexities of modern-day publishing. We will learn what happens to a book once it is written, the various roles professionals play to get it published, and why a writer needs an agent. We will cover editorial pitches, book design, and marketing and publicity. How does one find work in publishing? What are some new-age responsibilities of writers in an era of literature festivals and shameless self-promotion? How do some books become bestsellers while others fade into irrelevance? We will address all these questions via in-class lectures, seminars and meetings with professionals.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Life at Different Scales or Instructor approval
Description: The course is intended for second year undergraduate students and is meant to be an introduction to the physical and chemical principles that underlie and underpin the biology of organisms. The course will help students understand the molecular logic of life; it will enable them to find answers to questions pertaining to the various aspects of a biological system; these are some samples. How, in biological systems, is energy created or captured, stored, and transmuted, and how is the need for energy sensed? What are the energetic and kinetic bases of a biochemical reaction, which is in turn a unit of a physiological process? How are the various biomolecules synthesized and degraded, and how is the balance between anabolism and catabolism maintained? What are the guiding principles of this homeostasis? How are the various physiological processes orchestrated and synchronized at the level of the system? How does a bodily fluid such as blood act as a buffer, and how is this physiologically important? What are the various classes of biomolecules that make up molecular superstructures, and how do their structures help them perform their function? Instruction in the above will help the student to begin to learn to interpret experimental data, and to better understand biochemical research.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: At the discretion of the instructor
Description:
The course aims to bring together and synthesize the various concepts taught in the Biochemistry and Microbiology courses, to enable a better understanding of these subjects through practical application. The practicals will include instruction in basic laboratory procedures, such as the maintenance and use of a laboratory journal, acquaintance with basic laboratory rules and safety regulations, the preparation of solutions and buffers, the measurement of mass and pH, calculation of solution concentrations as normality, molarity, molality, or as mass/volume, volume/volume etc, the preparation of solutions and buffers, the estimation of error in measurements of mass, volume, pH and other variables*, the use of basic laboratory glassware/plasticware and instruments, the extraction and estimation of protein or DNA in solution, the use of the compound- and stereo-microscopes, the gram staining of bacteria, the preparation of bacterial media (Luria Bertani or another), the sterilization of labware and media, the preparation of culture plates, the inoculation and culture of media by various means, and the extraction and analysis of bacterial deoxyribonucleic acid by chromatography. The course may also include exercises in the laboratory using data drawn from the literature.
*Instruction in the estimation of error will be provided in PHYS lab classes intended for PHYS, CHEM, and BIOS students.

The course is designed for a college level audience, and is intended as a comprehensive foundation for advanced courses that students may opt for in the future. Course topics will be contemporary, and will focus on conceptual understanding and not encyclopedic detail. The course will involve the study of microbes of the various taxa, viz viruses, protozoans, bacteria, algae, and fungi, their place in the evolutionary order of things, their diversity and distribution, and their relevance in the Anthropocene. The course will use a bacterial-centric approach in its treatment of microbial taxonomy, metabolism, genetics, multiplication, and growth. Industrial, agricultural, environmental, and clinical applications and value will be highlighted wherever relevant using microbial archetypes; this will include certain clinically important pathogens and their control, fermentation as an industrial process, the use of engineered microbes in waste processing and pollution control, and agricultural pests and pest controls. The contribution of microbes to human health (as the microbiome, and as probiotics), and societal and environmental health (as degraders of waste) will be discussed. Students will be taught to isolate bacteria from their surroundings, and to examine, identify, propagate, and preserve them. Emphasis will be placed on bacterial genetics, especially the bacterial extra-chromosomal DNA (the plasmid) and its centricity in recombinant DNA techniques or genetic engineering. The course will enable the student to understand the multitudes of microbes cohabiting with humans, and the nature and degree of interaction between the two. Care will be taken to cross-reference concepts taught in this course with relevant concepts taught in earlier courses.

This course covers the fundamental principles of ecology and ecosystem dynamics, relating these with evolutionary processes and introducing concepts of disturbance and resilience. The focus is on the principles of life, how it functions at the population, community and ecosystem levels, relating these with adaptations to unique environmental conditions. This course will be split into four interrelated modules. The first module, population ecology, will deal with the fundamental concepts of habitat and niche, population dynamics (e.g., population growth and regulation) and population structure (e.g., metapopulations). The second module, community ecology, will focus on species interactions (e.g., interspecific competition, predation and mutualism), the nature of communities (e.g., community structure and function). The third module, ecosystem ecology, will take a in depth look at ecosystem structure and function (e.g., energy flow and nutrient cycling), ecosystem dynamics (e.g., ecological succession) and major concepts related to biogeography (e.g., the theory of island biogeography and the major biogeographical zones of India). The final module, conservation biology, will bring together the previous modules and show how the field of conservation biology has harnessed the principles of ecology to manage biodiversity. The course will focus on the principles of conservation (e.g., the design and management of protected areas), ecological restoration and will conclude with some important case studies, frorm India and across the globe, that showcase various conservation/management strategies.

Description: The course comprises a study of the human defense system against pathogens and disease causing agents. It will start with the genesis of the immune system from the lymphoid cells of bone-marrow tissue, and its maturation. It will go on to the molecular basis for determination of self- and non-self, and how an aberration in this process causes the immune system to go rogue and cause auto-immune disease. The course will center around the humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, of their attendant molecular and cellular events, and how the immune system evolves throughout the lifetime of an individual. It will address different aspects of the immune system such as the genetic control of immunoglobulin gene expression, and antibody production, maturation and diversity, and the roles of the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes. The modulation or suppression of the immune system for tissue and organ graft will be discussed, as will be the reciprocal effects of disease and the immune system, allergies and the inflammatory response, and the use of the immune-system as therapy against cancer and other diseases as drugs or vaccines. The course will also include the mechanisms pathogens have evolved to evade the immune system, and the state of our knowledge of these systems. The reconstitution of the human immune system in mice will be discussed at length to further enable the student’s understanding of the same.

This course is a primer to plant life, covering what comprises the plant Kingdom, how to identify different plants, and how plants reproduce. The first part of the course will explore the diversity of plants from algae to angiosperms. This will include discussions of plant evolution and phylogeny, how and when the first land plants arrived, how plants are classified, and how to identify broad groups of plants including some common Families of angiosperms. We will also explore morphological, anatomical, physiological and other adaptations of plants that allow them to grow in diverse environmental conditions. The second part of the course will focus on the different reproductive strategies of various groups of plants. Some aspects unique to plant reproduction will be discussed, such as alternation of generations in lower plants, and monoecy, dioecy, pollination strategies, double fertilization and embryogenesis in higher plants.

Description:
The Advanced Cell Biology course builds upon the foundational Cell and Molecular Biology course and is a deeper dive into the working of the cell in the context of a system. The course is a problem and exercise based approach to understanding specific aspects of the cell in the context of its physiological milieu and system (Human/Animal). The course will begin where the Basic cell and molecular biology (BIOS 205) course ended. This is an ideal and probably very important subject for students who want to pursue MSc/PhD and want to build a career in research in an academic or industrial setting. This course will connect with other areas of bioscience (microbiology, physiology, Immunology) to understand the connections between these related areas. It will delve into the cross talk among different cell types across tissue/organs and their role in health and diseases.
The syllabus include,
Visualizing and analyzing molecules, cells, and systems (contd from BIOS 205)
The Cell Cycle: its control and regulation; aberrations in its control and the consequent effect on the cell and system; growth, development, differentiation.
Cell death; apoptosis and programmed cell death, autophagy, senescence; stem cells and cell lineages
The evolution of the rogue cell and its contextual behavior
Cell signaling archetypes in eukaryotic cells and systems; their control and regulation; redundancy; defects in signaling systems and their ramifications, as in NCDs
Drug discovery and delivery : Current trends

Description: The cell is an integrated device made of several thousand types of proteins molecules, each of which is a molecular machine to carry out very precise tasks. The cell lives in a complex environment and must make decisions about input signals including temperature and osmostic pressure, biological signalling molecules from other cells, beneficial nutrients and harmful chemicals. Information about the internal state of the cell, such as the level of metabolites and cell damage is also important. The information processing functions, that is, responding to these signals, is largely carried out by the transcription factors and networks. In this course we will discuss the engineering principles of biological networks and their implications in cellular functioning and diseases.

Course Title: Introduction to two dimensional NMR spectrscopy
Description: This course provides an introduction to the principles and applications of two-dimensional (2D) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Students will learn the theoretical foundations of 2D NMR, including the concepts of spin interactions, coherence transfer, and pulse sequences. The course will cover key techniques such as COSY, HSQC, HMBC, and NOESY, with a focus on their utility in structural elucidation of organic and biomolecular compounds. Through a combination of lectures and problem-solving sessions, students will develop the ability to interpret 2D NMR spectra and apply these methods to solve complex structural problems in chemistry and biology.

Topics include the chemistry of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, water, and enzymes, along with their roles in food quality, nutrition, and stability. Students will explore the impact of processing, storage, and preparation on food chemistry and the development of flavor, color, and texture. Emphasis will be placed on understanding chemical reactions such as Maillard browning, lipid oxidation, and enzymatic activity, which influence both the safety and sensory properties of foods.

Topics include chirality, enantiomers, diastereomers, conformational analysis, stereoisomerism in organic and inorganic systems, and the influence of symmetry elements. The course emphasizes the role of stereochemistry in physical and chemical properties, reactivity, and biological activity, with examples from natural products, pharmaceuticals, and materials. Students will develop skills in visualizing and representing stereochemical relationships, and in applying stereochemical principles to predict molecular interactions and reaction outcomes.

Description:
This is an introductory course on applied dynamical systems for the data science major. The
 main aim of the discipline of dynamical systems is to model the phenomenon of dynamics or
 change that is ubiquitous in the real world. The earliest examples of dynamical systems
 addressed by humankind were the motion of planets and other celestial bodies, changes in
 seasons, and observations of the life cycles of plants and animals.
 Though it is impossible to track the change in each and every aspect of a given system with
 many dynamic parts, overall patterns persist that capture gross features of the system.
 Examples include periodic recurrences of phenomena, irreversibility of certain processes,
 and so on. The theoretical model of a dynamical system aims to capture such overall global
 features of the system in mathematically precise terms.
 An important idea that pervades the study of dynamical systems is chaos: the sensitivity of a
 dynamical system to initial conditions. The phenomenon of chaos is indeed the norm rather
 than the exception in the real world, and it appears in a variety of forms with different
 mechanisms as well. In this course, we will give an introduction to chaos and its importance
 in understanding the time dependence of real-world phenomena.
 A good understanding of the basic concepts in Calculus and Linear algebra is encouraged,
 but the course is designed to be self-contained and will include a review of the important and
 
 relevant concepts. The emphasis will be on visualizing the important ideas rather than on
 rigorous proofs. The course also aims to give a flavour of the interdisciplinary nature of the
 discipline via many case studies in biology, electric circuits, mechanics, finance, and so on.

Course Title: Climate Change: Science, Economics, and Policy
Description:
This course offers an in-depth exploration of global climate change, examining its scientific, economic, and policy dimensions. We will begin by discussing real-world manifestations of climate change and the fundamental science behind Earth's climate system. This includes understanding weather patterns, energy balance, the role of greenhouse gases, and the carbon cycle, along with future scenarios and tipping points.
 
 Students will engage with the latest scientific reports, such as those from the IPCC, to grasp observed and projected changes in climate. We will critically analyse issues of equity and responsibility in climate change. We will deconstruct the concept of “net-zero” emissions, discussing carbon budgets, sequestration techniques, the outcomes of international climate negotiations, and the geopolitics of climate change.
 
 In addition, the course covers practical aspects like carbon footprinting and the evaluation of real-world commitments to achieving carbon neutrality. We will study the impacts of climate change, including compound events, and explore both mitigation and adaptation strategies. Economic aspects such as carbon markets and various economic models will also be discussed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the approaches to addressing climate change.
 
 An overarching theme running through the course will be the issue of climate (in-)justice, which we will examine from multiple perspectives. The course will culminate in end-term projects, in which groups will synthesize and apply the knowledge gained throughout the course.

This multidisciplinary course provides a comprehensive and critical exploration of sustainability, focusing on the interconnectedness of its environmental, social, and economic dimensions. It examines the historical and scientific origins of the sustainability movement and its evolving principles, while critically assessing contemporary global challenges such as water scarcity, food insecurity, energy demands, rapid urbanization, pollution, waste management, and the impacts of war and violent conflict. It introduces sustainability frameworks and models and, through global examples and case studies, explores both actionable strategies and limitations for addressing sustainability challenges. The course engages critically with sustainability concepts and trade-offs, drawing from disciplines such as ecology, economics, ethics, and development studies. The course fosters reflection on the complex stakeholder interplay, values and behaviours of individuals and groups, examining concepts of power dynamics, inequality and social justice, and emphasizing their impact on individuals and communities.
