Description:
Theatre of the Climate: Performing a Just Future is an interdisciplinary course that
 bridges environmental sciences and the arts to explore climate change as both a systemic
 crisis and a human story. As climate realities become increasingly urgent, understanding
 them requires not only scientific insight but also emotional resonance, cultural memory, and
 ethical imagination. This course invites students to examine climate change through the
 lenses of social and ecological justice, considering how inequalities of caste, gender and
 geography shape vulnerability and responsibility.
 Blending systems thinking, ecological theory, and participatory art practices in theatre,
 dance, storytelling, and visual arts, students will explore the role of traditional knowledge
 systems, in making the climate crisis personal and public. Drawing on readings from
 science, performance studies, and decolonial thought, alongside engagements with artistic
 practitioners and community archives, students will develop original art-based interventions.
 The course culminates in collaborative performance prototypes that embody just and
 sustainable futures. It is ideal for students pursuing environmental sciences, global arts, or
 any other discipline with an interest in climate action and creative expression.
 Theatre, dance, and visual arts can bring to life the narratives of those affected by
 environmental injustices, offering audiences a visceral understanding of these complex
 issues.
 This course is proposed to be capped at 15 students.
 Learning Outcomes:
 1. Students will be able to analyse climate change as a “super wicked problem”
 using systems thinking and social-ecological frameworks.
 2. Students will critically engage with the intersections of climate injustice and
 social inequality through caste, gender and class lenses.
 3. Students will develop and apply performative, visual, and narrative art
 practices to sense, express, and communicate climate experiences and
 knowledge.
 4. Students will collaboratively design and present creative interventions - such
 as performances or installations - that address climate justice and imagine
 alternative futures.

This interdisciplinary course prepares prospective academics, activists, ethicists, leaders, researchers and policy-makers for environmental justice challenges and opportunities in India and across the world. The initial course module focuses on the theoretical foundations and conceptual contexts of environmental justice. Next, an experiential education module guides learners in developing familiarity with the practice of environmental justice. The concluding module on institutional and societal changes for environmental justice further develops and synthesises the theoretical and practical insights generated earlier in the course.
 
 Environmental justice - a discourse that straddles research, policy, and activism – focuses on the dynamics of justice/injustice in environment-related thinking and action. A crude definitional attempt would be to say that environmental justice is concerned with who wins and who loses in any given environmental context, why and how this happens, why this matters to those involved and to all of us, and what can be done to change things around. Further, good environmental justice theory is attentive to questions of difference and colonialism and the multiple crises of contemporary global capitalism; some political thinkers, for example, explicitly identify the goals of green politics as striking at the very heart of the polluted, materialist, consumerist, unequal, and industrial capitalist society. Concepts closely linked to justice, for example - equity, equality, fairness, responsibility, difference, recognition, liberty, dignity, violence, goodness, rightness, etc. - necessarily get included in any analysis of environmental justice.
 
 Making the quest for environmental and social justice a central concern requires confronting the fundamental underlying processes (and their associated power structures, social relations, institutional configurations, discourses, and belief systems) that generate environmental and social injustices. A coherent political account of how we could respond to these challenges requires the conceptual arsenal provided by environmental justice theory and practice. Ideas of environmental justice therefore enable “new critical engagements with the relations between economy, environment and society, and illuminate the radical potential of sustainability” (Harvey 1996). Such an approach gives environmental practitioners a suitably nuanced, historical, comparative, and ethical orientation for their specific practice. 
 Another question of relevance for this course is: what would distinctly non-Eurocentric environmental justice agendas for India and the global South look like? The analysis here could focus on questions such as: do vulnerable people in India suffer the most from current models of development? If so, why is this and what can be done to correct the situation? How can we balance the tension between economic development and environmental protection in specific Indian geographies? What might be the tensions and polarities between conservationists and resource-dependent communities? What kinds of movements, campaigns, programs and projects are successful in achieving environmental justice in the distinctively Indian contexts of unstable federalism, rampant poverty, violent state action, low literacy, identity and coalition politics, endemic official corruption, poor enforcement machinery, etc.? What can environmental justice practitioners in India learn from the global environmental justice movement and from movements in other places in the global South? 
 
 Summarizing the above discussion, an environmental justice approach as understood in this course, therefore: 
 critically, contextually and holistically re-examines the foundations of environmental/sustainability thinking and action from the standpoint of justice, and;
 applies the insights gained from such a critical re-examination to ethically devise, implement and evaluate new approaches and solutions to pressing socio-environmental problems. 
 
 The course enables learners to develop an 'environmental justice mindset' and to develop familiarity with some common approaches, methods, tools and resources to augment the practice of environmental justice in varied sectoral/disciplinary/professional contexts. The course will be built around specific exercises and experiential components focused on professional practice that responds to some key problems of environmental injustice. Workshop-style segments will focus on brainstorming, envisioning, strategising, design, research methodology, team-work, prototyping, documentation, fund-raising, and communication for professional practice relating to environmental justice.

Course Title: Writing in Mathematics and Quantitative Sciences
Description:
Writing and communicating mathematical ideas are becoming more and more important to practitioners of Mathematics and mathematically oriented sciences. While Mathematics is concerned with theorems and proofs, disciplines such as Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science, Economics, and Data Science additionally employ mathematical formalism for modeling and mathematical statistics for data analysis. Writing and communication in these disciplines take the form of research publications as well as writing in public forums in accessible language. This course explores writing and communicating mathematical knowledge in two distinct but related registers: technical and non-technical (specifically, journalistic) writing. The first register discusses how to convey mathematical ideas in the form of proofs, model derivations, and statistical analysis to a technically trained audience, while the second register explores how science journalists disseminate these ideas to a wider readership. In this course, the students will read exemplary pieces of academic and journalistic mathematical writing to derive principles of effective communication and implement the same in their
 own writing.

While Mathematics is concerned with theorems and proofs, disciplines such as Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science, Economics, and Data Science additionally employ mathematical formalism for modeling and mathematical statistics for data analysis. Writing and communication in these disciplines take the form of research publications as well as writing in public forums in accessible language. This course explores writing and communicating mathematical knowledge in two distinct but related registers: technical and non-technical (specifically, journalistic) writing. The first register discusses how to convey mathematical ideas in the form of proofs, model derivations, and statistical analysis to a technically trained audience, while the second register explores how science journalists disseminate these ideas to a wider readership. In this course, the students will read exemplary pieces of academic and journalistic mathematical writing to derive principles of effective communication and implement the same in their
 own writing.

Required for: 3 Year MATH Major, 4 Year MATH Major, Double Major with Mathematics as a Discipline
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Proofs and Ideas: An Introduction to Mathematical Thinking
Description: Groups are the mathematical formalisation of symmetry: in this course, students will study their definition and basic properties. In particular, the important notion of a group action will be introduced. Group theory provides an organizing framework for describing the internal symmetries of mathematical objects across many branches of mathematics, while also serving as a useful language for describing many mathematical invariants.

Required for: Required for 4 Year MATH Major, To be chosen from a basket of courses for 3 Year MATH Major, and Double Major with Mathematics as a Discipline
Description:
Topology is the study of spaces and sets and can be thought of as an extension of geometry. It involves the examination of the local as well as the global structure of a space or set. The foundation of General Topology (or Point-Set Topology) is set theory. There are other areas of topology including Geometric Topology, Algebraic Topology, Differential Topology, Low-Dimensional Topology, and various others. 
 
 This course provides a bridge between the basic knowledge of metric spaces and the more abstract knowledge of algebraic topology. In this course, we see how metric spaces can be generalized to objects called ‘topological spaces’ and the properties of metric spaces can be formulated in a more general way for these spaces. We will cover topological spaces, open and closed sets, interiors and boundaries of sets, continuous functions, homeomorphisms, connectedness, and compactness.
 After the completion of this course, a student should be able to:
 Define and illustrate the concept of topological spaces and continuous functions,
 Define and illustrate the concept of product topology and quotient topology,
 Prove a selection of theorems concerning topological spaces, continuous functions, product topologies, and quotient topologies,
 Define and illustrate the concepts of the separation axioms and countability axioms,
 Define connectedness and compactness, and prove a selection of related theorems.

Required for: Required for 4 Year MATH Major, To be chosen from a basket of courses for 3 Year MATH Major, and Double Major with Mathematics as a Discipline
Description: Probability is the branch of mathematics that deals with the study of randomness. The study of probability provides a foundation to systematically explore processes in the natural and social worlds around us. In this course students will be introduced to the basics of probability theory including the underlying axioms, conditional probability and independence, random variables, and distributions. The course will also cover proofs of some of the classic results in probability theory, the Weak Law of Large Numbers, and the Markov and Chebyshev inequalities. At the end of this course, students will have an appreciation for using mathematical formalism in exploring randomness, and develop a basic set of tools to rigorously model phenomena with underlying uncertainty.

Required for: 3 Year MATH Major, 4 Year MATH Major, Double Major and Minor with Mathematics as a Discipline
Description:
In this course, students will develop an understanding of the foundations of calculus. The course will provide a rigorous introduction to limits, continuity, differentiability, and integration, in the context of real-valued functions of a single real variable. Students will also be exposed to some of the applications of this material in the form of a short introduction to the Gamma function, a function with numerous applications in many branches of mathematics including mathematical physics, number theory, and probability. 
 After completing this course, students will have the ability to prove many of the fundamental theorems of calculus, thus providing a rigorous justification for results they may have seen previously in other circumstances. The material studied here is a fundamental part of any mathematician’s training: it will be used repeatedly throughout the rest of the mathematics major in a variety of courses.

Required for: To be chosen from a basket of 7 courses for a 4 year MATH major
Description: Surfaces are all around us, walls and ceilings of our rooms are planes, bottles are cylinders, the football in the playground is a sphere and the rugby ball is an ellipsoid, the vada we eat is a torus and the ice cream cone is, well, a cone. The shape of these objects will be studied using calculus. The course will begin with the study of curves in plane and in three-dimensional space. The concepts of length, orientation, speed, curvature, and torsion will be introduced and studied. Motivated by the study of curves, several notions of curvatures of a surface, like principal curvatures and Gaussian curvature, will be examined. Intuitively, the way a surface is curved seems to be a property of how it is embedded in space. But Gaussian curvature turns out to be intrinsic, that is, an ant confined to moving on the surface will be able to measure this quantity. This hints at the possibility of the study of shapes of higher dimensional analogues of surfaces.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Prerequisites include the basic notions of linear algebra (matrices, vector spaces and linear independence, linear transformations, eigenvalues and vectors and inner product spaces) and single and multivariable calculus.
Description:
This course is an introduction to the basic notions of Fourier analysis. Three classical topics will be explored: Fourier series, Fourier transforms and the discrete Fourier transform. The basic notions, tools and techniques of Fourier analysis are very important in both pure and applied mathematics (in areas such as signal, image and data processing, etc;) and in physics and computer science. This course is designed to be a gentle, concrete introduction to the subject, with a focus on basic examples and with an eye towards applications. 
 Prerequisites include the basic notions of linear algebra (matrices, vector spaces and linear independence, linear transformations, eigenvalues and vectors and inner product spaces) and single and multivariable calculus.
 It is hoped that this course will be accessible to 3rd year and 4th year students in mathematics, physics, computer science, and data science.

Required for: Required for ALL TYPE OF MAJORS (2nd yr)Elective for Physics Minor
Description: Mathematics has been the language to express the laws of physics. Students doing physics must be trained in mathematics. Almost every branch of mathematics has been found useful to physicists. This course builds on the foundations laid in Mathematical Methods I. In these courses, ideas from linear algebra, multivariable calculus, complex numbers, ordinary differential equations, partial differential equations and probability are discussed. It is not the purpose of this course to take the theorem-proof route which is of importance to mathematicians. Rather, it aims to cultivate a sense of thinking that has precision and rigour which are essential to physics, and a bent of mind to understand mathematical texts. Completing the two courses on mathematical methods will further equip students to access mathematical biology, econometrics, econophysics, data science and mathematical modelling.

Required for: Required course for physics major and open for 2nd/3rd/4th all ug years.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Mathematical Methods I or equivalent course
Description: Analytical methods are often inadequate to deal with real systems, whether in physics or economics or any data-driven field. The alternate route is to carry out numerical computations. In recent times, this has become an important tool to be learned by any budding physicist. Learning this early enables one to go beyond idealised problems. It gives them the freedom to take up more challenging problems. Needless to say, numerical solutions will motivate us to seek analytical solutions, at least in an approximate sense. The course will focus on numerical techniques to handle linear systems, ordinary differential equations, etc.

Course Title: Classical Physics: Energy and Force II
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Classical Physics: Energy and Force I
Description: We explore the applications of the laws of classical mechanics to a variety of dynamical systems, such as the motion of fluids (which allows for the flight of airplanes), the orbits of planets and other celestial bodies under the influence of gravity, and the movement of bodies in non-inertial frames (such as winds and ocean currents on the rotating earth). These form the basis for more advanced fields such as astronomy and climate science. Deeper questions about motion in inertial and non-inertial frames lead naturally to Einstein’s general theory of relativity.We explore the applications of the laws of classical mechanics to a variety of dynamical systems, such as the motion of fluids (which allows for the flight of airplanes), the orbits of planets and other celestial bodies under the influence of gravity, and the movement of bodies in non-inertial frames (such as winds and ocean currents on the rotating earth). These form the basis for more advanced fields such as astronomy and climate science. Deeper questions about motion in inertial and non-inertial frames lead naturally to Einstein’s general theory of relativity.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Quantum Physics, Energy and Entropy, Statistical Physics (recommended)
Description: Matter is in the realm of our direct experience. Matter exists in different forms. Most common forms are solid, liquid and gas. Other forms of matter could be defined as well. But even among the solids, we encounter variety. Some solids are fragile while others are strong. Many solids expand on heating while some shrink, some liquids flow easily while others are sticky, and so on. Also, matter changes from one state to another on altering external parameters such as the temperature, pressure, electric field, etc. There is an obvious need to go beyond cataloguing these properties. Seeking to understand the basis for this vast variety of properties should be interesting, and could lead to innovations. For instance, the origins for revolution in information technology can be traced back to the availability of semiconductor transistors. This course introduces matter and its forms using the conceptual framework of physics.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Classical Physics- Energy and Force I
Description: This course discusses some inherent properties of matter such as surface tension, viscosity, fluid dynamics, elasticity, and various elastic constants. It also discusses the variation of these properties with temperature, pressure, and shape. The basic understanding of these topics is helpful for our day-to-day life as well. The knowledge about the above-mentioned topics can bring openings for research in nonlinear dynamics, soil research, and many interdisciplinary engineering domains, especially if somebody wishes to move into the career path of engineering physics such as civil engineering, fluid engineering, etc. Apart from this, a general knowledge about fluids, beams is helpful in many day to day events of life as well, such as why milk spills easily in a carrying container but not oil. In a nutshell, the students studying this elective course can benefit from having more career paths in the future.

Required for: Elective course for math major, minor & concentration
Description: There is plenty of room at the bottom” is a succinct expression by Feynman about the richness of the quantum world. How do we harness this abundance? In this course, we attempt to answer this question. Peter Shor designing a quantum search algorithm that is much faster than any known classical algorithm marked the beginning of a new paradigm. The most relevant aspect is the way we process information. Doing it the quantum way speeds up the process, makes it more efficient and surpasses, in many cases, the limits known from a classical perspective. This course begins with a discussion on information theory and introduces ideas about quantum information processing (QIP). Other topics to be covered include quantum algorithms and their experimental implementations. Students will learn to program the IBM quantum computer as well. Major corporates in IT and many leading institutes have strong research programs in QIP. That vouches for the importance of this science.

This course provides the basic knowledge of interaction of light with matter in terms of the relationship with the molecular structure. An overview of the various types of molecular motion and how they can be recorded using optical spectroscopic techniques will be discussed in some detail. In addition, students will be performing experiments using spectroscopy apparatus available on campus.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course:
Classical field theory (recommended), 
Quantum Physics II
Description: The Standard Model of Particle Physics is the most successful model of physics that describes the Universe at the most fundamental scales. In this model, the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions between matter particles are described by their mediation through vector bosons. The predictions of this model have been experimentally verified to high precision. While the Standard Model unifies electromagnetism and the weak force into a single electroweak interaction, research aims to achieve ‘grand unification’ including the strong interaction too. This course introduces the Standard Model through gauge theory and particle phenomenology, and involves calculation of various observed processes using Feynman diagrams.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: States of matter (PHYS316) or equivalent course
Description:
Over the past century, condensed matter physics has evolved from a nascent discipline into
 one of the most influential pillars of modern science and technology. Today, it is integral to
 countless aspects of contemporary life—shaping innovations in memory devices, electric
 vehicles, advanced battery materials, medical imaging technologies, alternative energy
 solutions, and experimental tools for both astronomers and particle physicists. This
 remarkable growth has been driven by the study of how materials respond to diverse
 external stimuli such as temperature, pressure, and electric or magnetic fields. This course
 offers a strong foundation in the theoretical framework of condensed matter physics,
 complemented by an introduction to key experimental techniques. By integrating these
 perspectives, it equips young researchers with both a broad overview of the field and the
 insight needed to choose impactful research directions aimed at sustainable solutions to
 global challenges.

Required for: This is a required course for all majors and minors
Description:
What factors determine student grades? What is correlation between student attendance and grades? Does breakfast improve attention? The answer to these questions is not factual but requires evidence which involves gathering data from a sample and then synthesizing the information using a relevant statistic to draw conclusions. We leverage statistical tools and techniques to gather evidence. This course offers an overview of the research process, use of scientific methods, research designs and the role of theory in psychological research. Students will further gain hands-on experience in analyzing real data using statistical analysis like measures of central tendency, t-statistics, ANOVAs & correlations.

Students will learn between-subjects and within-subjects design, the basics of descriptive statistics, including measures of central tendency, dispersion, surveys, such as probability, scales and their uses, ANOVA. The course exercises will rely on hands-on exercises using statistical packages to explore, visualize and analyze these data. Students will delve into hypothesis testing, probability theory, and the concept of statistical significance. Further, they will learn about various sampling methods, considerations of sampling biases, and the complexities of generalizing research findings to broader populations. A student emerging from this course will not only be equipped to use these tools and apply them, but also evaluate any ‘scientific evidence’ critically and judiciously. The students will learn to report and present data in a meaningful way, and learn to transform it into different visualization formats and demonstrate an understanding of experimental design. This course provides the foundation for the more advanced Statistics and Research Methods II (PSYC 209).

This course provides an in-depth exploration of the internal processes involved in perceiving, interpreting, and responding to the environment. Students will examine various cognitive processes, including perception, attention, learning, memory, language, problem-solving, reasoning, and thinking. Through a combination of theoretical discussions, experimental demonstrations, and empirical studies, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how these processes influence human behavior

This course will build social psychological foundations for the sociality of the self, interpersonal relationships, and group behaviour in Psychology. This will serve three important and interconnected purposes. Firstly, students will learn to think about social psychological research and some of the classic studies in nuanced and complex ways. Secondly, students will learn to critically appraise the work and findings of social psychological concepts reported in public discourse. Finally, students will learn to expand their concepts of the self as social beings with multiple social identities and bring these to bear upon their interpretation of social behaviour. The course will bridge the gap between simplified concepts in standard social psychology textbooks and the rigour, complexity and uncertainty of findings in the primary literature, including, among others, journals and theses.

This course will introduce learners to the ways that clinical psychologists approach the  conceptualization, assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of mental health problems. This course will provide an overview of the scientific study of mental illness (also known as
psychopathology). We will cover basic concepts and definitions, historical perspectives on psychopathology, different theoretical models of psychopathology, the assessment and diagnosis of mental illness, and research methods for studying mental disorders. The rest of the course will concern the leading categories of mental disorders among adults, children and adolescents, including the description and classification of these disorders, the leading theories and evidence explaining their origins, and some of the treatments for these disorders. Legal and ethical issues pertaining to the assessment and treatment of mental illness will be discussed, as well as the role of culture and diversity in assessment and treatment

This course introduces students to social, economic, and political dimensions of gender and sexuality with the goal of understanding how the diversity of these two aspects of the human experience impacts psychology and its allied disciplines. We will take a multi-disciplinary approach to explore, in particular: (i) differences and interrelationships between sex, gender, and sexuality; (ii) the relevance of cultural contexts to understanding human variation, especially as regards family, subjectivity, the politics of identification, and the impact of the predominance of ‘WEIRD’ research; (iii) theories of the performative aspects of gender and sexuality and the relevance of labour to gender and sexual roles and identifications; (iv) problems of categorisation and classification of normalcy and pathology, contemporary views on variation in biology, and the historical legacies of pathologisation of women and gender and sexual minorities; (v) problems in the public circulation and communication of specialist research (including overgeneralisation and misrepresentation of scientific findings and clinical practice); and (vi) some contemporary approaches in psychology research and practice that build on these social understandings. Students will gain experience in understanding how gender and sexuality are operationalised in psychology and its related fields of psychiatry and social work in both research and practice, as well as the tools to critically evaluate the promises and limitations of individual research studies by considering them in these broader contexts.

This interdisciplinary course starts from an introduction to psychophysics with its definitions, historical background and its intersection with neuroscience, psychology, physics and other interwoven disciplines. Examples from every day and real-life instances will make it more interesting. Adopting an interactive approach, this course will provide an overview of human sensory systems like vision, hearing, touch, taste, and smell and their neural basis. The students will learn about difference between the sensation and perception, responses and their qualitative and quantitative responses to various stimuli. As this course includes the experimental and data analysis aspects, students will not only learn about the data organization but also about its visualization and analysis.

This course is designed to introduce students to theories in Counselling. Along with the emergence of Psychology as a discipline that was studying the human mind, Counselling as a practice was also emerging. Through Counselling, Psychology was offering the ways and means to work with human beings in psychological distress. Within Psychology, Counselling is the field that not only offers an application of various understandings of the mind, but also an important purpose to the vast knowledge that it generates. The history of counselling is rich and dynamic. It has been influenced by social, political and intellectual movements at various times. This course aims to familiarize the students with this complex past and present of counselling through some of the major theoretical streams that developed within Psychology.

This advanced undergraduate course offers an interdisciplinary introduction to Critical Disability and Inclusion Studies (CDIS), foregrounding disability as a socially constructed and politically mediated category. Moving beyond individual and medicalized understandings, the course approaches disability through frameworks rooted in social justice, political economy, and intersectionality.
We begin by examining the historical and cultural construction of disability and ableism, alongside the emergence of critical theories of access, normalcy, and inclusion. The course then explores how developmental norms shape understandings of childhood disability, and how inclusive education can be reimagined through both psychological and pedagogical models. In the clinical module, we turn to psychiatric disability, community mental health, and cultural critiques of diagnosis and medicalization.
Intersectional concerns—such as gender, caste, sexuality, age, and race—are woven throughout, enabling students to critically engage with how multiple forms of marginalization structure experiences of disability. We also examine institutional practices, with case studies of inclusion efforts in higher education, such as at Krea University. The course concludes with an analysis of legal frameworks and policy debates in India and globally, grounded in the history of the disability rights movement.

Students will engage critically with theory, policy, and practice to design more inclusive and just systems.

Course Title: Counselling Skills: putting theories into practice (Formerly known as 'Helping Skills')
Description: This course is designed to provide an introduction to psychotherapy skills. Students will be able to understand elements of ethical and effective counselling practice. They will be able to identify and use various helping Skills at a beginner level with an appreciation of personal and sociocultural factors. The course also aims to enhance students' understanding of self as a tool and increase self-awareness and self-reflective abilities. Students will practice helping skills with each other every week. Attendance is mandatory and contributes to the course grade. Note that the course will involve discussing and working with emotionally charged content. Students should also be prepared to reflect on and talk about (not mandated) some personal/emotional issues in class.
